items.title: Avakian George — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: He got Clark Terry and Booker Ervin. I can’t remember who else. But the album is there, Joe Williams at Newport.

ctx.x: Joe, I felt, is the greatest male singer of all time, after Louis Armstrong. I always have to put Louis first, because he’s in a class by himself. He’s the daddy, like Billie Holiday. “I’m as close as I can get to Louis Armstrong,” she would say. Joe was the absolute professional all the way. It was a delight to record him. We recorded him in two contexts at RCA. One was studio dates, with Jimmy Jones, his favorite arranger. Those sessions went off beautifully, because everything was totally professional. We…

items.title: George Avakian interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 21, 1998
items.q: He would have Clark Terry for one or two nights... his sets were like a kind of history of jazz

ctx.x: I’m sorry, the younger white musicians?

The younger black musicians, did I say white? The younger black musicians don’t know the origins of jazz and they don’t know say the New Orleans tradition except for those who are down in New Orleans. A great example of the positive side of a young black musician knowing the foundation of the music is Nicholas Payton. I consider Nicholas to be the outstanding young jazz musician in the world today, by a considerable margin, and one reason is that he not only knows the music from the beginning on, but he can play…
goodness, and that was the duet album with Doc Cheatham and the performance of “Stardust.” I can’t even talk about it.
